**If a household sample shows lower bills under a different electricity plan, how can we tell whether the average saving is more than sampling noise?** A positive estimate is useful, but its precision matters: another sample could produce a different answer. This simulation follows one question through a bootstrap interval, a coverage experiment and a hypothesis test.

All households here are **simulated**. Define saving as the old-plan bill minus the new-plan bill for the same monthly usage, including fees. Positive values favor switching. I generate independent savings from a normal distribution with a **$3 population mean** and **$20 standard deviation**. Negative savings are possible. Knowing the truth lets us check the methods; these are not estimates for an actual electricity provider.

## What can one sample tell us?

The default sample contains **200 households**, with mean saving **`r money(case$mean)`**. To estimate uncertainty, draw 200 observations **with replacement** from those same households and calculate their mean. Repeat 9,999 times. A household can appear several times in one resample, while another is absent. Figure 1 plots these means—not individual bills.

For a **95% percentile bootstrap interval**, take the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of that distribution. Here the interval is **`r money(default$low)` to `r money(default$high)`**. It spans zero, so the positive estimate comes with uncertainty about the sign of average savings. The [bootstrap procedure](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.stats.bootstrap.html) reuses available observations; it does not collect additional households.

Use the controls to change all three figures. A higher confidence level widens the interval and lowers the test’s significance threshold. Changing sample size changes the observations too: a larger sample generally improves precision, but its estimated mean can move.

```{r}
#| results: asis
fragment('controls.html')
fragment('bootstrap.html')
```

## Does 95% mean the interval usually catches the truth?

Now repeat the **whole experiment**, drawing 2,000 fresh household samples. For each, construct a new interval using 999 bootstrap resamples. This outer repetition differs from resampling the original dataset: it checks how the procedure behaves across datasets.

At the default settings, **`r default$covered` of 2,000 intervals contain $3: `r percent(default$coverage)`**, close to the 95% target. Figure 2 displays the first 100 in their original order. The population mean stays fixed while the intervals move. “95% confidence” describes repeated coverage, not a 95% probability assigned to the fixed mean after observing one interval.

Coverage is approximate. With 50 households, the same procedure covers **`r percent(all_data$cases[['50']]$levels[['95']]$coverage)`** of the time in these simulations. More bootstrap draws can stabilize the calculation, but cannot supply information missing from a small household sample.

```{r}
#| results: asis
fragment('coverage.html')
```

## How surprising is this sample if average saving is zero?

Test **zero population mean** against a difference in either direction. Use $t=\bar{x}/(s/\sqrt{n})$, where $s$ is the sample standard deviation: the estimated saving measured in standard-error units. The default observed statistic is **`r sprintf('%.2f',case$t)`**.

Generate **50,000 new samples under zero average saving**, retaining the normal model and $20 spread, and calculate each t statistic. This is the null distribution in Figure 3. At a 5% significance level, reject when $|t|$ exceeds approximately **`r sprintf('%.2f',default$critical)`**: the two rejection tails together contain about 5% of null statistics.

The [Monte Carlo p-value](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.stats.monte_carlo_test.html) counts null statistics at least as far from zero as the observed one. With a small correction that prevents reporting zero, it is **`r sprintf('%.3f',case$p)`**. We therefore do not reject zero at 5%. Changing the confidence level moves the rejection boundaries, while this sample’s p-value remains unchanged. Switch the shading to compare p-value tails with rejection regions. The p-value is not the probability that zero saving is true.

```{r}
#| results: asis
fragment('null.html')
```

## Takeaway

The default sample estimates positive savings but does not reject zero—even though its simulated population really saves $3 on average. Failing to reject is therefore not evidence that savings are absent. The interval shows the sample’s uncertainty; repeated coverage checks the interval procedure; the null simulation measures surprise under zero. None turns a population average into a promise for every household.
